title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.4.4: Connect Wikis and Document Systems to a Knowledge Base
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.4.4: Connect Wikis and Document Systems to a Knowledge Base

A hands-on lab with a custom data source and direct ingestion into Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Task 1.4, post 4 of 6.

[IMAGE: cover-1-4-4.png — alt: "Skill 1.4.4: Connecting wikis and document systems"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.4: Design and implement vector store solutions · Post 4 of 6. Hands-on lab, about 25 minutes.

The policies customers read are in S3. The rules support agents follow are somewhere else: an internal wiki, Confluence, SharePoint. An assistant that only knows the S3 documents can tell a customer the returns window but not who is allowed to approve their refund. This skill is about connecting those other systems to a knowledge base, with as little custom code as possible.

What AWS says

Skill 1.4.4: Use AWS services to create integration components to connect with resources (for example, document management systems, knowledge bases, internal wikis for comprehensive data integration in GenAI applications).

What it means in plain words

Get content from the systems where people actually write it into your vector store, keep it current, and keep track of where it came from. There are four ways to do it:

[IMAGE: t1-4-4-connectors.png — alt: "Connecting sources to a knowledge base: built-in connector, export to S3, custom data source with direct ingestion, Amazon Q Business"]

  • Built-in connectors: Knowledge Bases can read Amazon S3, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce and websites (Web Crawler) directly. You configure them in the console; credentials go in AWS Secrets Manager.
  • Export to S3: a Lambda function or Glue job pulls from any system with an API and writes files to S3, which a knowledge base then syncs.
  • Custom data source with direct ingestion: your code pushes documents (or deletes them) straight into the knowledge base by ID, with metadata. No files, no full sync.
  • Amazon Q Business: when the goal is a ready-made assistant over many company apps, it brings 40+ connectors that respect each user's permissions in the source.

What we're going to do

The lab's wiki is home-grown, so there's no built-in connector. You'll write the small piece of code a connector needs:

  1. Add a CUSTOM data source called internal-wiki to the aip-lab-kb knowledge base from the Skill 1.4.2 lab.
  2. Map four exported wiki pages to knowledge base documents with metadata, and push them in.
  3. Check each page's indexing status.
  4. Ask a question across the whole knowledge base, then only across the wiki.
  5. Delete an outdated page by ID.

What you'll learn

  • When to use a built-in connector and when to write your own.
  • How direct ingestion works: documents, stable IDs and inline metadata.
  • How to filter retrieval to one source.
  • How to remove a single document without a sync.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 25 minutes, a few cents
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; the aip-lab-kb knowledge base and its KB_ID from the Skill 1.4.2 lab
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.4/skill-1.4.4-connectors

The lab

Step 1: Add a custom data source

export KB_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
python wiki_connector.py create
export WIKI_DS_ID=XXXXXXXXXX     # printed by the step above

A knowledge base can have several data sources. This one has type CUSTOM: it has no location to crawl, and accepts only what your code sends it.

Step 2: Map wiki pages to documents and push them

wiki_export.json holds four pages as a wiki's API would return them: two on refunds and returns labels, one on damaged items, one from the warehouse space. The connector turns each page into a document:

"custom": {
    "customDocumentIdentifier": {"id": page["id"]},     # e.g. wiki-102
    "sourceType": "IN_LINE",
    "inlineContent": {"type": "TEXT", "textContent": {"data": title + body}},
},
"metadata": {"type": "IN_LINE_ATTRIBUTE", "inlineAttributes": [
    source="wiki", space=..., title=..., published=20260112 ]}
python wiki_connector.py ingest

The ID is the important part. It's the wiki's own page ID, so if the page changes, pushing it again with the same ID replaces the old version instead of adding a duplicate.

Step 3: Check the status

python wiki_connector.py status

Ingestion is asynchronous. Repeat until every page shows INDEXED; usually a few seconds. A page that fails shows a reason here.

Step 4: Ask

python wiki_connector.py ask

The question is “Who has to approve a $500 refund?”. Across the whole knowledge base, the “Refund approval limits” page should come first, mixed with returns policies from S3. With the filter source = wiki, only wiki pages come back. The answer is on that page: refunds from $200 to $1,000 need a team lead.

The source attribute is how one knowledge base serves different audiences: an agent-facing assistant searches everything, a customer-facing one filters out internal wiki pages.

Step 5: Delete an outdated page

python wiki_connector.py delete
python wiki_connector.py status

Page wiki-103 describes last year's holiday returns labels. Deleting it by ID removes its chunks from the index straight away. No sync, no other pages touched. A real connector would do this when the page is deleted or archived in the wiki.

Built-in connectors in practice

For Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce or a public website, don't write this code. Add a data source of that type in the console, store its credentials in Secrets Manager, choose which spaces, sites or URL patterns to include, and sync on a schedule. The custom data source is for systems without a connector, or for changes that must appear within seconds.

Common pitfalls

  • Duplicates after re-ingesting: the document ID changed. Use the source system's stable ID.
  • Status shows FAILED: check the reason; empty text and wrong attribute types are the usual causes.
  • Expecting a sync to pick up wiki changes: a custom data source has no location to read. It changes only when your connector calls ingest or delete.
  • Credentials in code or environment variables: connectors read them from Secrets Manager; your own connector should too.

Clean up

Keep the internal-wiki data source for the Skill 1.4.5 lab, or delete it: Knowledge Bases → aip-lab-kb → Data sources → internal-wiki → Delete.

What to remember

  • Built-in connector first: S3, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, Web Crawler.
  • No connector → a custom data source with direct ingestion, or export to S3 with Lambda or Glue.
  • Direct ingestion pushes and deletes documents by ID in seconds, without a full sync.
  • Use the source system's stable ID, and attach metadata such as source so retrieval can be filtered by origin.
  • Connector credentials belong in AWS Secrets Manager.
  • A ready-made assistant over many apps with per-user permissions → Amazon Q Business.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 6 of this task: Task 1.4 Exam Notes.
